To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

NMT embeddings outperform monolingual embeddings on tasks requiring knowledge of semantic similarity or lexical–syntatic role; that these desirable properties of N MT embeddings should emerge largely indepen- dently of the source and the target languages; and that NMT embeddings can be made available for a large vocabulary of 100,000 words.

(1) NMT embeddings are better at capturing semantic and syntactic similarity than monolingual embeddings, and (2) this effect can be observed in both the target language of the translation task and the source language.

(1) NMT embeddings are better than monolingual embeddings at capturing semantic similarity and lexical function (e.g. antonymy), but worse at capturing nonspecific word relatedness; (2) NMT embeddings can be trained on large vocabularies without sacrificing quality; (3) NMT embeddings trained on large vocabulaires are available for download.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NMT embeddings are superior to monolingual embeddings on tasks that require word meanings to be organized according to lexical function and/or semantic similarity.
the NMT embeddings are better suited for semantic similarity and/or syntactic role, while monolingually trained embeddings are better suited at modelling (nonspecifc) inter-word relations.

NMT word embeddings are better than word embeddings from monolingual texts in terms of the quality of word meaning representation, while monolingul word embeddings have a better quality of word-word relatedness representation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NMT models learn a better geometric representation of words than other word embedding models.
NMT word embeddings are a promising alternative to monolingual word embeddings, and should be used in tasks requiring knowledge of lexical–semantic and lexical–syntatic roles.
word embeddings learned by NMT models are more similar to those learned from monoligual texts than previously thought, but they are still different enough to be useful for different tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the representational geometry of NMT embeddings is more suitable than that of monolingual embeddings for modelling the semantic structure of word concepts, and that this is largely independent of the source and the target language.
NMT word embeddings have the desirable properties of being able to encode both semantic and syntactic knowledge, while also being able to capture the full range of linguistic variation.
NMT models can learn useful representations of words that go beyond the information present in the training data.
